opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few ways to read that result, and they're not mutually exclusive.

The first, and probably most charitable, interpretation is that it reflects something real about the task. Machine learning research is a very open-ended, creative activity. It involves deciding which questions are worth asking, noticing when an anomalous result is actually interesting rather than a bug, integrating intuitions from many subfields, and making judgment calls under a lot of uncertainty. If you think of automation as proceeding from well-specified, narrow tasks toward ill-specified, general ones, then it's natural to put "do frontier AI research" near the end of the list. It's almost definitionally one of the hardest cognitive tasks, because to fully automate it you need a system that's roughly as capable as the best researchers.

But I'm wary of taking that at face value, for a couple of reasons.

One is that experts tend to be most attuned to the difficulty of their own work. When you're an ML researcher, you see all the tacit knowledge, the dead ends, the taste that goes into a good paper, and you're less exposed to the equivalent complexity in, say, surgery or law or truck driving. So there's a plausible "my job is special" bias. We see this pattern across many professions: people systematically think their own domain is harder to automate than outsiders do.

A second reason is that the question decomposes. "Automating ML research" isn't one switch that flips. Big chunks of the research pipeline, like writing code, running and debugging experiments, hyperparameter search, literature review, drafting papers, are already being substantially accelerated by AI tools. You don't need full automation for there to be a feedback loop where AI meaningfully speeds up AI progress. So even if the last 10% of the job, the research taste and agenda-setting, is among the last things to go, the acceleration could kick in much earlier than the headline survey answer would suggest.

And that's really why this matters so much from a governance perspective. AI automating AI research is one of the key mechanisms by which you could get very rapid, potentially discontinuous capability gains, the kind of dynamic that would compress the time society has to notice problems, build institutions, and respond. If people anchor on "ML research gets automated last," they might infer that we'll see plenty of warning, with everything else automated first and lots of time to adjust. I think that's a risky inference. Partial automation of research, concentrated in a few frontier labs, could shift the pace in ways that aren't very visible from outside.

There's also a general point about these surveys: the answers are quite sensitive to framing. We've seen large differences depending on whether you ask about "tasks" versus "occupations," or ask for a year versus a probability by a given year. So I'd treat any specific ordering as soft evidence. The robust takeaway for me is that there's a lot of uncertainty, the experts themselves put meaningful probability on fairly near-term transformative capabilities, and the research-automation feedback loop is something we should be monitoring closely rather than assuming is far off.

r001.rationale: The response discusses forecasts that ML research will be automated later than other tasks, but does not compare that timing with human-level AI.

r002.rationale: It says ML researchers may see their own work as unusually hard to automate because they know its tacit knowledge and complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I find that result really interesting, and I think there are a few ways to read it. The context is the survey Katja Grace and I and colleagues did of machine learning researchers, where we asked about when various tasks would be automated. And one of the striking findings was that respondents put AI research itself quite late — later than things like truck driving, retail work, writing a bestselling novel, even surgery in some framings. That's a bit surprising if you take the view that AI research is a fairly cognitive, computer-based, well-specified task compared to something like surgery, which involves fine motor control and messy physical environments.

So one interpretation is that there's a kind of bias at work, where people tend to think the thing they do is especially hard. Everyone's job looks more complicated from the inside, because you see all the tacit knowledge, the judgement calls, the taste involved in picking good problems. Machine learning researchers are no exception. They look at their own work and see a lot of creativity and intuition, and they look at a surgeon's work and see a well-defined procedure. The surgeon would probably say the opposite. So I'd put some weight on that just being a general feature of how people assess automatability.

A second interpretation is more substantive, which is that they might actually be right. Doing good research involves things that are quite hard to formalise: choosing what questions matter, forming intuitions about why an approach might work, communicating with the community, integrating lots of weak signals. These might genuinely be among the harder capabilities to get. And there's an argument that the economic incentive to automate some of these other tasks is larger and more immediate, so even if they're comparably difficult in some abstract sense, we'd see them automated first.

But I think the finding matters a lot for how we think about the trajectory of AI, because the automation of AI research is exactly the thing that in a lot of models of rapid progress — the intelligence explosion scenarios — is the key feedback loop. If AI systems can substantially contribute to improving AI systems, you'd expect progress to accelerate. So if experts think that's one of the last things to be automated, that suggests they expect a more gradual, broad transformation of the economy before you get that kind of feedback. Alternatively, if they're wrong about it, and AI research turns out to be automatable relatively early, then you could get a world where the feedback loop kicks in before the rest of society has adjusted to AI, which is a more worrying scenario from a governance perspective.

So I don't think we should take the exact ordering too literally. These are very uncertain forecasts, the respondents gave wildly different answers depending on how the question was framed, and expert predictions in this area have a mixed track record. But I think it's a useful data point, both as a reflection of how researchers see their own work, and as something to keep in mind when thinking about which scenarios of AI development we should be preparing for.

r001.rationale: The response says respondents placed AI research later than several other tasks, but does not compare its automation with human-level AI.

r002.rationale: It suggests researchers may see their own work as especially hard to automate because they experience its tacit knowledge, judgment, and creativity firsthand.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about taking that ordering too literally. One possibility is that researchers know how difficult their own work is. They see all the judgment and creativity involved in doing machine learning research, whereas they may have a much more simplified picture of what other people do. So they can imagine those other tasks being automated while finding it harder to imagine their own work being automated.

But there’s also an important distinction between automating all of machine learning research and automating enough of it to accelerate progress. You could still have humans choosing research directions and interpreting results, while AI systems do much of the coding and experimentation. That could substantially speed up AI development well before an expert would say, “Machine learning research has been automated.”

So I wouldn’t read those predictions as strong reassurance that AI won’t accelerate its own development until after almost everything else has been automated. The partial automation along the way could be very consequential.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts automation of machine learning research with other tasks, but does not mention surveyed experts predicting it will happen later than human-level AI.

r002.rationale: It suggests researchers see the judgment and creativity in their own work, making them less able to imagine it being automated than other people’s work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are at least two interpretations. One is that machine learning research really is unusually difficult to automate. It involves figuring out which questions to ask, designing experiments, and making judgments about what the results mean. So perhaps experts are identifying something important about the difficulty of their own work.

The other interpretation is that people have a tendency to see their own work as especially difficult to automate. You know all the subtleties of what you do, whereas someone else’s job can look like a fairly straightforward collection of tasks. So I’d be cautious about treating that prediction as strong evidence that machine learning research will actually be among the last things automated.

And it’s a particularly consequential uncertainty, because automating machine learning research could accelerate AI progress itself. You wouldn’t necessarily need to automate every part of a researcher’s job for that to matter. If AI systems substantially speed up experiments or help generate better ideas, that could already change the pace of development.
